notes.meaning: Moses and the leaders of the tribes speak together and tell the people to keep all of God's commands. This is the only place in Deuteronomy where the elders speak alongside Moses. Moses would not cross the Jordan River, but these leaders would. So they would be the ones to make sure God's law was obeyed in the new land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think two different openings to the chapter have been joined together here, and that an editor later arranged verses 2-7.

notes.meaning: Once Israel crossed into the land, they were to set up big stones and cover them with plaster. "On the day" means "around that time." It was actually done some days after the crossing. The plaster gave a smooth, bright surface, so words written on it were easy to see and read. This was a way of writing that was used in Egypt.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older Catholic commentary notes that one ancient version speaks of just two stones. It takes the words written on them to be only the Ten Commandments.

notes.meaning: God's law was to be written on the stones as Israel entered the good land He had promised. Teachers differ on how much was written. Some say the Ten Commandments, some the blessings and curses, and some a larger part of Deuteronomy. Setting the law up at the edge of the land showed that the land belonged to God's service. Because Canaan was a gift from God, Israel would keep it by obeying Him.

The stones were to stand on Mount Ebal, the mountain where the curses would be spoken. Placing the law there showed that breaking it brings a curse. It also showed that no one can be made right with God just by keeping the law. The sacrifices offered there pointed ahead to the only way out from under that curse: Christ's death for us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Samaritan version of the first five books of the Bible says "Mount Gerizim" here instead of "Mount Ebal." Some scholars think that was the original wording. Many older commentators believe it was changed on purpose.

notes.meaning: Next to the written law, Israel was to build an altar. They had to use rough stones that no iron tool had shaped, and offer burnt offerings on it. Through the law God spoke to His people, and through the altar they spoke to Him. So God's word and prayer go together. Normally there was to be only one altar for the whole nation. This one was simple because God ordered it for a special, short-term occasion. Many have seen in the uncut stones a picture of Christ, the "stone cut out without hands."

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: One writer mentions a rough stone altar found on Mount Ebal from around Joshua's time. He suggests iron was avoided because it was seen as foreign or linked with other gods.

notes.meaning: They were also to offer peace offerings, which were thank-you gifts. They were to eat them there and celebrate before the LORD. This was the one kind of offering the worshipper could eat. The shared meal sealed the covenant (a binding agreement with God), as the meal at Mount Sinai had done. It showed the people's joy in being God's people.

The words had to be written clearly, so that everyone could read and understand them. No one could then claim they did not know God's law. Those who teach God's word today should also make it as plain as they can.

Moses and the priests call for silence and attention. "Today you have become the people of the LORD" because the covenant was being renewed with this new generation. Being God's own people was a great gift, and it brought a duty with it. Because God had chosen them, they were to obey His voice and keep His commands.

On that same day Moses gave more instructions. God wanted His promises and warnings to sink deep into the people's hearts. So they would not only hear them spoken but also agree to them out loud. Joshua later carried this out, as Joshua 8 records.

The twelve tribes were split into two groups. One group stood on Mount Gerizim for the blessing and the other on Mount Ebal for the curse. The two mountains faced each other across a valley near Shechem. The Gerizim tribes came from Jacob's wives Leah and Rachel. The Ebal tribes came mostly from the two servant women, plus Reuben, who had lost his place as firstborn, and Zebulun, Leah's youngest. "Joseph" stands for his two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. Since all spoke for the whole nation, the exact split mattered less than their shared agreement.

The priests who carried the ark stood in the valley between the two mountains and called out loudly. They spoke God's words as if God Himself were speaking. Only the curses are written down here, not the blessings. Many have seen in this a hint that the law alone can only condemn. Blessing would come through Christ, whose Sermon on the Mount begins with blessings.

The first curse falls on anyone who makes an idol and hides it away, even in secret. "Cursed is" states a fact about God's judgment rather than wishing harm. The verse covers every wrong done against God's worship. A hidden idol might escape human judges, but not God. When the people said "Amen" ("so be it"), they agreed that God's warning was true and fair.

This curse is on anyone who treats father or mother with contempt. Open abuse of parents was punished by the courts. But a scornful heart toward parents is something only God sees. So God places it under His own curse. It goes against the command to honor your parents.

Moving a boundary stone meant secretly stealing a neighbor's land. It breaks the command against stealing. It stands for every kind of cheating and taking what belongs to others. Some teachers apply it today to honesty in business.

Leading a blind person off the road is a cruel trick on someone who cannot see. Teachers apply it more widely to giving harmful advice to someone who trusts you. It also covers failing to help a neighbor in need. Leading others into sin falls under this warning too.

This curse is on anyone who twists justice against foreigners, orphans, or widows. These people often had no one to stand up for them. Judges might be tempted to side against them because nothing could be gained by helping them. But God Himself is their protector.

Sleeping with your father's wife (a stepmother) is a deep wrong against your father. It is a wicked act done against him. Reuben had done this very thing, and his tribe stood on Ebal. Such sins brought not only the courts' punishment but God's anger.
Sexual acts with an animal are also put under God's curse. Such shameful acts are usually kept carefully hidden. But God warns that no hiding place will help. In the end He will bring them to light.

These curses forbid sex with a sister or half-sister, and with a mother-in-law (your wife's mother). Sins like these were often done in secret. The people's "Amen" showed their horror at them. The same laws appear in Leviticus 18.

This curse is on anyone who kills a neighbor in secret, for example by poison or an ambush. The victim never gets a chance to defend himself. Such a murder might never be found out by people. But God, who sees in secret, will judge it.

This curse is on anyone paid to bring about an innocent person's death. It includes being bribed to accuse, convict, or condemn someone in court. Using the law itself to commit murder is a great insult to God. Such secret deals are hard for courts to uncover, but God sees them.

The last curse covers everyone who does not live out the whole law. It includes the good we fail to do as well as the evil we do. The sins listed before were only examples. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:10 to show that no one keeps God's law perfectly, so all stand under its curse. The only rescue is Christ, who took the curse on Himself for us.
